analysis.one_liner: Guarantees train crews 72 hours off after working seven straight days.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote: it died in a House subcommittee with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred railroads from forcing a train employee who has been on duty or on call every day for seven days straight back to work until at least 72 hours have passed since the worker was released. It was meant to prevent fatigue among train crews, a safety issue for workers and the public riding on or living near rail lines. It never moved past referral to a subcommittee.
analysis.who_benefits: Train crews — engineers, conductors, and other train service employees — who would gain a guaranteed three-day rest block after a week of continuous duty or availability. Rail passengers and communities near rail lines would also benefit from better-rested crews.

how_it_helps.text: Adds a new limit to federal rail law: a railroad may not require an employee who has been on duty or available for any part of seven consecutive days to work or be on call until at least 72 consecutive hours have passed after release [S3].
The CRS summary describes this as an additional hours-of-service limitation on railroad carriers and their officers and agents [S2].
The bill's subjects include hours of labor, occupational health and safety, and railroad safety, indicating its purpose was fatigue protection for train employees [S1].

analysis.who_pays: Railroad carriers, which would lose scheduling flexibility and would have to hold or reassign crews to cover the mandatory 72-hour rest periods, potentially raising operating costs.

drawbacks.text: The 72-hour break applies after any seven consecutive days on duty or merely available for duty, so railroads argued-style objections would center on the cost and disruption of holding crews out for three days, especially for workers on call rather than actively working [S3].
The bill contained no exception for emergencies or crew shortages, so a railroad short-staffed after a week of disruptions would have to operate without the affected employees for 72 hours [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety benefit of guaranteed rest for fatigued crews is substantial and aimed at a group with little scheduling control over their own lives, while the cost falls on railroads' scheduling flexibility. The bill was simple and narrow, though its lack of emergency exceptions would have created real operational strain during service disruptions.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, and then sent to its Railroads Subcommittee, where it sat with no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steven LaTourette introduced the bill on July 23, 2001, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure [S1].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Railroads, where no further action is recorded [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action appears in the action history before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Railroad carriers came out ahead: they kept full scheduling control over train crews with no mandatory 72-hour rest requirement, and the members of Congress who chose not to advance the bill faced no vote on it.

for.name: Rep. Steven C. LaTourette
for.role: Sponsor, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only supporter of record; it was referred to a committee on which he served

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough for votes or recorded opposition; it simply had no cosponsors of either party [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have cost railroads scheduling flexibility by requiring a 72-hour rest block for any crew member on duty or call seven days straight. Its death left railroads free to keep crews on duty or on call indefinitely under existing hours-of-service limits.
